entries.name: Family Alliance Ontario
entries.description: Family Alliance Ontario is a family-based non-profit for families who support a person with a developmental disability. It connects families to affiliated local family networks and shares articles on planning ahead, including wills, trusts and estate planning for the time when parents are no longer here.
entries.cost_note: Membership is offered; no fees are listed on the pages checked.
entries.address: 20-850 King Street West Oshawa, Ontario L1J 8N5
entries.evidence: This article invites you to think about planning ahead and having the right legal tools in place to ensure a quality of life for your loved one when you are no longer here.
entries.notes: Mailing address is c/o Durham Family Network. The board page lists elections on October 4, 2026, so the organisation is active. The estate-planning item links out to a Henson trust article; Family Alliance does not give legal advice itself. The email is the organisation's general address.

entries.name: Free online webcasts (Partners for Planning)
entries.description: Partners for Planning, a charity founded by families and based in Toronto, runs free online webcasts for families supporting a relative with a disability, on wills and estate planning, Henson trusts and the RDSP. The wills session explains trusts and the two types of power of attorney, comes with a free workbook, and invites families to virtual discussion groups.
entries.cost_note: Webcasts and resources are free.
entries.address: 290 Carlaw Ave Suite 207 Toronto, ON M4M 3L1
entries.evidence: If you're supporting a family member with a disability, one of the most important steps you can take to help secure their future is to create a will and estate plan.
entries.notes: Upcoming dates seen in October 2026: Wills and Estate Planning (Oct 28, 2026), Introduction to the RDSP (Nov 5 and Dec 7), The Henson Trust (Nov 10). Partners for Planning's Henson Trust resource page is already a ResourceHub listing (e5ded037-6e94-421d-83bf-ca7490788625); this entry is the webcast series, so no existing_id was set.

entries.name: Professional Services Directory (Partners for Planning)
entries.description: An online, Ontario-wide directory from Partners for Planning that lists lawyers, financial advisors and accountants with working knowledge of disability-related issues. It is meant for families who have had trouble finding qualified professionals to help with legal and financial planning for a relative with a disability.
entries.cost_note: Free to search; the professionals listed are separate businesses and Partners for Planning does not endorse them.
entries.address: 290 Carlaw Ave Suite 207 Toronto, ON M4M 3L1
entries.evidence: Many families have told us about their difficulty in accessing qualified professionals to handle disability-related issues. In response P4P has developed a province-wide, online Professional Services Directory.
entries.notes: The directory map loads with JavaScript, so individual listings were not checked. Partners for Planning states it does not vet or endorse the providers listed.

entries.name: Independent Facilitation (Partners for Planning)
entries.description: A trained facilitator from Partners for Planning works with a person with a disability and their family over time to build a vision for the future, expand their personal network and plan the steps toward a safe and secure future. It is fee-for-service, can be done virtually, and Special Services at Home (SSAH) or Passport funding can be used to pay for it.
entries.cost_note: Fee-for-service; SSAH and Passport funding can be used.
entries.address: 290 Carlaw Ave Suite 207 Toronto, ON M4M 3L1
entries.evidence: Independent Facilitation is an ongoing process that supports an individual with a disability to develop a vision for their future and to take the steps necessary to work towards their dreams.
entries.notes: Facilitators are listed for the Markham, Muskoka, York Region, Niagara and Hamilton areas. The page says families in a crisis should not start facilitation at that time.

entries.name: Find an Independent Facilitator (Ontario Independent Facilitation Network)
entries.description: The Ontario Independent Facilitation Network is a community of people with developmental disabilities, families and independent facilitators. Its online listings and guidance (things to consider, questions to ask) help families find a facilitator who works with the person and family over time to plan for the future and build the everyday life they want.
entries.cost_note: OIFN does not set fees; arrangements are made directly with each facilitator.
entries.evidence: Independent facilitators work with people and families over time, assisting people to tell their stories, identify and work on action steps, and reflect on learning and new possibilities as they come into their adult lives.
entries.notes: Only 4 facilitator listings were shown when checked, and OIFN does not vet or endorse listed facilitators. Partners for Planning says Passport and SSAH funding can pay for facilitation.

entries.name: Microboards Ontario
entries.description: Microboards Ontario helps families set up a Microboard: a small not-for-profit corporation of family and friends formed with a person with a developmental disability to help them plan, make decisions and stay connected. Parents use it to plan for support when they can no longer provide it, and it offers workshops, peer mentors and step-by-step help with incorporation.
entries.cost_note: Incorporation support program is free to families except about $220 for incorporation and a NUANS name search; insurance is about $900-1,400 a year.
entries.evidence: A Microboard is a group of committed family and friends who join with a person with a developmental disability to create a supportive not-for-profit corporation.
entries.notes: Upcoming presentations listed for Oct 20 and Nov 7 (year not shown); a pilot for families of children 18 and under is open. Costs are from the FAQ, which also says a Microboard is not guardianship and has no legal authority over the person's life. Contact is by web form only.

entries.name: Safe and Secure Ontario Edition (Partners for Planning and Plan Institute)
entries.description: A free planning guidebook for Ontario families of a person with a disability, prepared by Partners for Planning from PLAN's Safe and Secure. It walks through seven practical steps, with fillable worksheets, to build a financial, legal and social plan so the family member stays safe and supported, including for the times parents cannot be there.
entries.cost_note: Free to read online; the PDF is $0.00 on the Plan Institute store.
entries.evidence: With a blueprint in place—financially, legally, and socially—you will feel more prepared for the future, even for the times when you cannot be there.
entries.notes: Ontario edition funded by the Law Foundation of Ontario. The book is a product (guide), not a service; Partners for Planning runs the related webcasts and facilitation listed separately.

entries.name: Safe & Secure Futures Networks (Extend-A-Family Toronto)
entries.description: Monthly online meetings, facilitated by Extend-A-Family Toronto from September to June, where families learn to build a support circle of family and friends around a relative with a disability. Guided discussions cover transition planning, person-directed planning, creating the right place to live, and financial and estate planning, with resource parents sharing their experience.
entries.cost_note: Not stated; funded by a City of Toronto Community Services Grant.
entries.evidence: Safe & Secure Futures Networks (facilitated by Extend-A-Family) aim to empower families to develop and nurture a support circle with their family member who has a disability.
entries.notes: Extend-A-Family Toronto's Family Support Groups are already listed (4d845435-761c-48e8-b41d-25a472f869a2); this is a different program, so no existing_id. Meeting details are sent on request; the facilitator's direct line on the page is a named person's, so the office number is given.

entries.name: Make a power of attorney (Ministry of the Attorney General, Ontario)
entries.description: Ontario's guide to naming someone you trust to make property (financial) or personal care decisions if you cannot, with a free power of attorney kit and a free online form-builder from Community Legal Education Ontario. Parents use it to plan who will act for them, and an adult with a disability who is able to make one can choose a trusted family member so family does not have to go to court to become guardian.
entries.cost_note: Free kit and free CLEO online Guided Pathway; using a lawyer is optional and paid.
entries.evidence: Without an attorney for property, your family, including your spouse, cannot automatically step in to make financial decisions for you. They might have to go to court to become your court-appointed guardian.
entries.notes: General government page, not disability-specific (updated October 14, 2025). A person must be mentally capable to make a power of attorney: 18+ for property, 16+ for personal care. The CLEO Guided Pathway builds the documents for free; CLEO, OPGT and Guardianship are already listed separately.

entries.name: Residential supports for adults with developmental disabilities (Government of Ontario)
entries.description: Ontario's page on funded services for adults with a developmental disability, including residential supports (group living, supported independent living, specialized supports and the Host Family Program) and Adult Protective Service Workers for adults living on their own. Families planning a future home work with their local Developmental Services Ontario office, whose housing coordinators and navigators help explore options.
entries.cost_note: Government-funded services; eligibility and access go through Developmental Services Ontario.
entries.evidence: Developmental Services Ontario offices have housing coordinators and navigators to help you explore housing options in your community
entries.notes: Page updated April 13, 2026. Developmental Services Ontario and Passport are already listed separately; this entry is for the residential supports, Host Family Program and APSW information on this page. Passport funding can also pay for person-directed planning.

entries.name: I Decide Law Program (PooranLaw)
entries.description: A province-wide pro bono program from the law firm PooranLaw for Ontario residents with an intellectual disability and/or acquired brain injury who are financially eligible. It helps people make their own powers of attorney and wills (wills at reduced rates), challenge guardianship and do person-directed planning, using plain-language materials.
entries.cost_note: Pro bono for financially eligible clients; wills at reduced rates.
entries.address: 1500 Don Mills Road, Suite 400, Toronto, Ontario M3B 3K4
entries.evidence: We advocate for the decision-making rights of people who have intellectual disabilities. Through legal education and direct services, we aim to promote self-directed decisions and future planning.
entries.notes: PooranLaw is a private law firm (a business); this is its free pro bono program. Eligibility: Ontario residents who are financially eligible and have an intellectual disability and/or acquired brain injury. The firm also has a Windsor office (7025 Enterprise Way).

entries.name: Trust & Estate Planning (PooranLaw)
entries.description: A law firm whose services for families include wills and powers of attorney, Henson trusts, Qualified Disability Trusts and Lifetime Benefit Trusts for a family member with a disability, RDSPs and Disability Tax Credit eligibility. It can also act as a professional estate trustee or trustee of a Henson trust.
entries.cost_note: Private law firm; fees are not listed.
entries.address: 1500 Don Mills Road, Suite 400, Toronto, Ontario M3B 3K4
entries.evidence: Establishing a Henson Trust, Qualified Disability Trust and/or Lifetime Benefit Trust for your family member with a disability – whether now (inter vivos trust) or upon death (testamentary trust)
entries.notes: This is a business (law firm). Its principal lawyer, Brendon Pooran, also presents the free Partners for Planning and Plan Institute wills webinars. Offices in Toronto and Windsor.

entries.name: Reach Legal Referral Services (ABLE2)
entries.description: ABLE2, an Ottawa disability charity, connects people with disabilities in the Ottawa and Champlain regions with volunteer lawyers, paralegals and mediators for a one-time, confidential consultation on a legal issue. If no match is available, it points people to other community services that may help.
entries.cost_note: One-time consultation with a volunteer legal professional; any further work is a separate arrangement with that lawyer.
entries.evidence: Reach Legal Referral Services connects people with disabilities in the Ottawa and Champlain regions with volunteer lawyers, paralegals, and mediators for legal information and advice.
entries.notes: Referrals by online form or phone only; a match is not guaranteed. Covers any legal issue, not only wills or planning. ABLE2 is fundraising to keep the service running in 2027 (Access to Justice campaign, goal by December 31, 2026). ABLE2 lists a PO box and says it moved to remote operations, so no street address is given.

entries.name: Financial planning for parents of a child with a disability (Kindred Credit Union)
entries.description: An Ontario credit union's guide for parents of a child with a disability: applying for the Disability Tax Credit, opening an RDSP, Henson trusts, ODSP rules, and life insurance, wills and powers of attorney for parent and child. It invites parents to meet its Wealth and Investment team to plan a secure future for their child.
entries.cost_note: A business (credit union); fees for advice are not listed.
entries.evidence: Meet with a member of our Wealth and Investment team to discuss how Kindred can help you create a secure future for your child.
entries.notes: Business (credit union). Article dated September 22, 2025. Several Kindred branches are already listed as Bank places; this entry is for the planning service, not a branch, so no existing_id.

entries.name: Planning for the Future: Government Funding for Adults (Autism Ontario)
entries.description: Autism Ontario's planning page for autistic adults and their families, explaining ODSP, Passport, the Disability Tax Credit, the Canada Disability Benefit, the RDSP and Henson trusts in plain terms. It links to Partners for Planning, ConnectABILITY, PooranLaw and Microboards Ontario for planning help.
entries.cost_note: Information page; no cost stated.
entries.evidence: The most well-known and commonly used Trust among families of people with disabilities is the Absolute Discretionary Trust, more commonly known as the "Henson" Trust.
entries.notes: Autism Ontario's Awards and Funding page is already listed (7dbf3adf-023e-4e89-ba92-fb5823892f0a); this is its separate 'Planning for the Future' sub-page, so no existing_id. Information only; planning help comes from the organisations it links to.

entries.name: Journey to Adulthood workshops (Autism Ontario)
entries.description: Autism Ontario's online workshops for parents and caregivers of autistic youth moving into adulthood: a 90-minute overview for families of youth aged 12 to 18, offered about four times a year, and a six-week discussion workshop for parents of youth aged 15 to 19 covering funding, consent and capacity, legal issues and community connections. A downloadable Journey to Adulthood portfolio has folders for legal and financial papers and emergency care information.
entries.cost_note: Not stated.
entries.evidence: Topics may include funding, consent capacity and legal issues, post secondary options, building community connections, employment, and advocacy.
entries.notes: The six-week workshop is usually offered in fall, winter and spring and has a waitlist. Autism Ontario's Awards and Funding page is already listed (7dbf3adf-023e-4e89-ba92-fb5823892f0a); this is a different program, so no existing_id.

entries.name: Henson Trusts and guardianship for families (Kenneth C. Pope Law)
entries.description: An Ottawa law practice that concentrates on helping families with a member who has special needs plan for the future: wills with Henson trusts that protect ODSP eligibility, and adult guardianship applications. Its Henson trust page explains in plain terms how the trust works with ODSP and what it costs to set up and run.
entries.cost_note: Legal fees to draft the trust in a will and later to set it up; a paid trustee usually takes 1-1.5% of assets a year.
entries.evidence: Pope, principal of Kenneth C. Pope Law, concentrates his practice in areas that help families who have members with special needs to access funding and plan for their future.
entries.notes: This is a business (law firm). It accepts clients from across Ontario and Canada and offers a short courtesy assessment through a Family Evaluation form. The practice profile is an older reprinted article (site footer says 2016); the Henson trust page cites the current ODSP limits ($40,000 assets, $10,000 a year from a trust).

entries.name: RDSP.com (Plan Institute)
entries.description: Plan Institute's free website on the Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP) for people with disabilities and their families across Canada: a tutorial and step-by-step guide, an RDSP calculator, a list of banks and credit unions that offer the plan, and free online RDSP and Disability Tax Credit webinars with live Q&A.
entries.cost_note: All services are free.
entries.evidence: It was created to provide families and professionals across Canada with the most accurate and up-to-date information available on the RDSP. All of our services are free and are intended to help people become informed and to support future planning initiatives.
entries.notes: Webinar dates seen: RDSP Level 2 on Oct 20, 2026 and Level 1 on Nov 24, 2026 (Pacific Time). The list of financial institutions is not complete, and grant and bond income thresholds on the site may be out of date. The government RDSP page and Plan Institute's Disability Planning Helpline are already listed. Phone is Plan Institute's workshops line.

entries.name: Free DTC application support (Partners for Planning)
entries.description: Partners for Planning gives free one-on-one help to people with disabilities and their families to apply for the Disability Tax Credit (DTC), which unlocks the RDSP and the Canada Disability Benefit. The same page lists other free, federally funded DTC navigators across Canada by region and community.
entries.cost_note: Free.
entries.evidence: Partners for Planning provides free, personalized navigation support to help people with disabilities and their families apply for the Disability Tax Credit (DTC) and unlock related federal benefits, such as the RDSP.
entries.notes: Federally funded; the page lists Partners for Planning under national organizations. Inclusion Canada's Barrier-Free Benefits navigators and Plan Institute's helpline, also on that list, are already in ResourceHub.

entries.name: Personal Support Network Facilitation online course (Plan Institute)
entries.description: A self-paced online course (25 to 30 hours within six weeks, with no set log-in times) that teaches PLAN's approach to building a personal support network of caring relationships around someone who is isolated, including a person with a disability. It is open to family members and caregivers of a loved one with a disability, as well as workers.
entries.cost_note: $300 per seat (5 seats for $1,200); an inclusion fund can help people who cannot afford it.
entries.evidence: However, the course is open to anyone, including family members and caregivers who have a loved-one with a disability.
entries.notes: 2027 dates were 'coming soon' when checked (October 2026). Certificate of completion. Phone is Plan Institute's workshops line.

entries.name: Thinking ahead for beneficiaries with disabilities (RBC Wealth Management)
entries.description: A guide from RBC Wealth Management for families making an estate plan when a family member has a disability. It compares a Henson trust with a Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP), including taxes, effects on provincial disability benefits and leaving RRSP or RRIF money to an RDSP, and links to finding an RBC advisor.
entries.cost_note: Article is free to read; RBC Wealth Management is a business and advisor fees are not listed.
entries.evidence: When a family member has a disability, estate planning may be more complex. Here are two potential options to consider.
entries.notes: Business (a bank's wealth-management arm); an advice article rather than a free service. It tells readers to consult qualified tax and legal advisors and notes that a Henson trust may not be recognized in every province.

entries.name: Tax and Finance Collection (AIDE Canada)
entries.description: A national online collection from AIDE Canada, the autism and intellectual disability knowledge network, on benefits, taxes and future planning. Its future-planning section has recorded webinars on estate planning for a loved one with a disability (wills, Henson trusts, powers of attorney and building a support network), an aging caregiver's toolkit from Autism Calgary, and a finance guide for adults who have a sibling with a disability.
entries.cost_note: Online resources; no cost stated.
entries.evidence: "What will happen to our children once we have gone?" This Webinar will focus on the valuable endeavor of how parents can plan for the legal and social aspects for their children's future.
entries.notes: AIDE Canada itself is already listed (259891ae-7a91-4704-923b-16cbb3bc33d5 and 529558b2-d0c8-4f97-adc1-3835e664bbc6); this is a specific resource collection, so no existing_id. The estate-planning infosheet in it is Ontario-specific. AIDE staff answer questions by live chat (9am AST to 5pm PST, Monday to Friday).

entries.name: Planning and Advocacy (Planned Lifetime Advocacy Network)
entries.description: PLAN is a Vancouver family-led organisation whose mission is to help families secure the future for a relative with a disability. Its Family Advocate helps families, including siblings, navigate government ministries, funding, housing options and legal systems, and mobilize formal and informal networks around their relative.
entries.cost_note: Not stated; PLAN offers a Lifetime Membership.
entries.address: 101-1001 West Broadway Vancouver, British Columbia V6H 4E4
entries.evidence: Providing families with peace of mind about the future, knowing their loved ones will be safe, secure, and supported for the rest of their lives.
entries.notes: PLAN's team meets families in community spaces throughout the Lower Mainland; the Vancouver address is a mailing address. The email on the page is hidden by spam protection, so none is given.

entries.name: Personal Support Networks (Planned Lifetime Advocacy Network)
entries.description: PLAN works with people with disabilities and their families in the Lower Mainland to build a personal support network of trusted friends, neighbours and community members around the person. Network members are prepared over time to take on roles like advocacy and decision-making as family circumstances change, so the person is not left isolated.
entries.cost_note: Not stated.
entries.address: 101-1001 West Broadway Vancouver, British Columbia V6H 4E4
entries.evidence: Planning for the Future: We help prepare network members to take on roles like advocacy and decision-making as family dynamics evolve.
entries.notes: Same organisation as the Planning and Advocacy entry; contact through the Vancouver office.

entries.name: Future Planning (PLAN Okanagan)
entries.description: PLAN Okanagan runs recurring future-planning workshops, in person and online across the Okanagan, for families of people with disabilities: RDSPs, wills, trusts and estates, and succession plans of care, plus book-club sessions on the Safe and Secure guide. In October 2026 it listed a free wills, trusts and estates workshop in Kelowna and an RDSP workshop with Autism BC.
entries.cost_note: The October 2026 wills, trusts and estates workshop is free; other workshop costs are not stated.
entries.evidence: Do you have a succession plan of care for your loved ones? PLAN Okanagan can help with this difficult question and more.
entries.notes: Workshops listed on the home page for October 2026 (RDSP workshop on Oct 27, 2026); registration is through zeffy.com links. Listed as a Plan Institute affiliate.

entries.name: Microboard support (Vela Canada)
entries.description: Vela Canada helps families in British Columbia set up a Microboard: a non-profit society of at least five family members and friends formed with a person with a disability to help them plan their life, advocate for what they need and make sure services are safe. It also helps with person-led planning, funding proposals and becoming an employer of support workers.
entries.cost_note: There is no charge for Vela's services in British Columbia.
entries.evidence: A Microboard is a small (micro) group of committed family and friends (a minimum of 5 people) who join together with a person with a disability to create a non-profit society (board).
entries.notes: Funded in part by Community Living BC. No street address on the pages checked; email is hidden by spam protection.

entries.name: Section 7 Representation Agreement (Nidus Personal Planning Resource Centre)
entries.description: Nidus is a BC charity that gives free information, forms and support for Representation Agreements, the BC legal document that lets an adult name trusted people to help with decisions. The Section 7 agreement (RA7) is for adults whose capability is in question, with autism, FASD and developmental disability among its examples, and many families make one when their son or daughter turns 19 and parental rights end.
entries.cost_note: Free forms, information and support.
entries.evidence: Many people with a disability from birth or childhood make an RA7 when they become an adult (age 19), because parental rights end
entries.notes: Nidus has no physical office (mailing address in Abbotsford only). BC law only. Nidus also runs the Nidus Registry for storing planning documents (not checked).

entries.name: Wills, Trusts, and Estate Planning in BC Webinar (Plan Institute)
entries.description: An online webinar from Plan Institute for families and caregivers of a loved one with a disability in British Columbia, with a live Q&A with a disability lawyer and a parent. It covers writing a will when a family member has a disability, protecting them when family passes away, discretionary and other trusts, and the roles of executors and trustees.
entries.cost_note: Price not stated; registration is limited to 60 people.
entries.evidence: Ways in which to ensure your loved one with a disability is protected when family passes away
entries.notes: Dates seen: Nov 26 and Dec 10, 2026 (Pacific Time). Focuses on BC law. Phone is Plan Institute's workshops line.

entries.name: Lifetime Networks
entries.description: A Victoria, BC charity started in 1998 by parents of children with developmental disabilities who wanted to know what would happen to their child when they were gone. It builds Personal Support Networks of three or four unpaid friends, guided by a facilitator and meant to last the person's lifetime, and also offers outreach support for people living on their own and respite.
entries.cost_note: Fees are conditional upon circumstances.
entries.evidence: Lifetime Networks began in 1998, created by five caring families seeking to secure a bright future for their children with developmental disabilities. They asked: "What will happen to my child when I am no longer here?"
entries.notes: No referral needed (the About page says it is open to everyone without a referral process). Not the same as the former Lifetime Networks program in Ottawa.

entries.name: Services for adults (Public Guardian and Trustee of British Columbia)
entries.description: BC's Public Guardian and Trustee protects the legal, financial, personal and health care interests of adults who need help with decision making and have no one else to help. Its pages explain adult guardianship law and the personal planning tools adults can use ahead of time, and give information and support tools to private committees.
entries.cost_note: The PGT has a fees page for some services; amounts not checked.
entries.evidence: We provide a range of services to adults who may need help managing their personal, legal and financial affairs and do not have other decision makers available to help them.
entries.notes: Toll-free 1-877-511-4111. Not disability-specific; for planning ahead in BC, Nidus (Representation Agreements) is listed separately.

entries.name: Adult guardianship (Office of the Public Guardian and Trustee, Alberta)
entries.description: Alberta's Office of the Public Guardian and Trustee explains how a family member can apply to court to become guardian (personal decisions) or trustee (financial decisions) for an adult who cannot make their own decisions. Parents of a teen with a disability who will need a decision-maker as an adult can apply soon after the teen turns 17 so the order starts at 18.
entries.cost_note: Court filing fee up to $300, plus capacity assessment and background check costs; a hardship application can cover some costs.
entries.address: 4th Floor, John E. Brownlee Building, 10365 97 Street
entries.evidence: If you want the court order to go into effect when the minor turns 18, you must apply as soon as possible after the minor turns 17.
entries.notes: Updates to Alberta's Adult Guardianship and Trusteeship Act took effect April 1, 2026 (OPGT main page). Less restrictive options, such as supported decision-making, must be considered first. Phone and address are the Edmonton main office (adult guardianship); Calgary and other offices are on the contact page.

entries.name: Supported decision-making (Office of the Public Guardian and Trustee, Alberta)
entries.description: In Alberta, an adult who can make their own decisions but wants help can sign a Supported Decision-Making Authorization naming one to three trusted people, such as a relative or friend, to help them get information and communicate personal, non-financial decisions. The adult stays in charge and can end it at any time; it is one of Alberta's alternatives to guardianship.
entries.cost_note: No fee is mentioned; the authorization is a form the adult and supporters sign.
entries.evidence: Even if an adult is capable of making decisions, there may be times when they need someone to help them make personal decisions not related to financial matters. This is called supported decision-making.
entries.notes: Supporters cannot be the adult's guardian or trustee. Listed by the OPGT under alternate personal decision-making options for adults.

entries.name: Future Planning and Advocacy (PLAN Calgary)
entries.description: PLAN Calgary works with a family to create a tailor-made Future Plan for a relative with a disability, starting from the family's wishes and worries for the future. Each plan covers financial stability, a place to call home, decision-making, meaningful contribution and a personal support network of lifelong relationships.
entries.cost_note: Not stated; PLAN Calgary offers memberships.
entries.evidence: PLAN Calgary is able to provide a unique Future Planning model for people with disabilities. It is an in-depth process completed with families to create a safe and secure future for their loved one.
entries.notes: Listed as a Plan Institute affiliate. Also offers personal networks of support and family support (separate pages).

entries.name: Transition to Adulthood (Autism Calgary)
entries.description: Autism Calgary's planning timeline for Alberta families of autistic teens and teens with developmental disabilities who are turning 18: apply to Persons with Developmental Disabilities (PDD) at 16, for adult guardianship and trusteeship at 17, and for AISH or ADAP income support at 17 and a half. It explains capacity assessments, guardianship, trusteeship, the RDSP and the Disability Tax Credit in plain terms.
entries.cost_note: Information page; no cost stated.
entries.address: 3639 26 Street NE, Suite A, Calgary AB, T1Y 5E1
entries.evidence: At age 18, individuals must transition from FSCD to adult programs like PDD and Disability Income Assistance (AISH/ADAP). Because wait times are long, families must plan early to prevent gaps in support.
entries.notes: Autism Calgary is already listed (22f77417-dd80-4056-a8cd-15bf8a4b5bce), as are its Family Support and Peer Support Groups pages; this is its separate transition-planning page, so no existing_id. Alberta-specific.

entries.name: Guardianship and Co-decision-making for Dependent Adults (Government of Saskatchewan)
entries.description: Saskatchewan's page on how a person 18 or older, such as a parent, can apply to the Court of King's Bench to become a guardian, or a co-decision-maker for an adult who needs help with decisions but not a guardian; under this law an adult is anyone 16 or older. A self-help kit with the forms is provided and the Public Guardian and Trustee answers questions.
entries.cost_note: Not stated.
entries.evidence: a personal or property co-decision-maker for adults requiring assistance in decision-making but who do not require guardians
entries.notes: Contact details are the Public Guardian and Trustee's (mailing address). Applications go to the Court of King's Bench. Not disability-specific.

entries.name: Office of the Commissioner for Adults Living with an Intellectual Disability (CALIDO)
entries.description: Manitoba's office that decides, as a last resort, whether an adult with an intellectual disability needs a substitute decision maker for personal care or property, appoints and monitors them, and reviews the need at set intervals. It also gives adults, their families and support networks information about how substitute decision making works.
entries.cost_note: Not stated.
entries.evidence: In certain situations, adults living with an intellectual disability require someone who is legally empowered to make decisions on their behalf, known as a substitute decision maker.
entries.notes: Covers adults whose intellectual disability began before age 18, under The Adults Living with an Intellectual Disability Act. The old /fs/vpco/ web address now redirects here. Toll-free 1-800-757-9857. The email is the office's general address.

entries.name: Public Guardian and Trustee of Manitoba
entries.description: Manitoba's Public Guardian and Trustee manages the estates of, and makes personal decisions for, adults living with an intellectual disability who are not able to make decisions on their own, and manages trust money for people under 18 or under a legal disability. It also acts for people who name it in a power of attorney and handles estates when no one else is able or willing to.
entries.cost_note: The office has a fees page; amounts not checked.
entries.evidence: Administers estates and makes personal decisions on behalf of mentally incompetent adults or adults living with an intellectual disability who are not mentally capable of making decisions independently.
entries.notes: Brandon office 204-726-7025; toll-free 800-282-8069. Substitute decision makers for adults with an intellectual disability are appointed through CALIDO (listed separately).

entries.name: Assistance measure (Curateur public du Québec)
entries.description: A free Quebec measure that lets an adult who lives with a difficulty, such as a mild intellectual disability, have one or two trusted people officially recognized by the Curateur public as assistants. The assistants help the adult make decisions, deal with service providers and manage their property, while the adult keeps full control over their own decisions.
entries.cost_note: Free of charge.
entries.evidence: The assistance measure allows a person experiencing a difficulty to be assisted free of charge by one or two people of their choice while keeping full control over their decisions.
entries.notes: The adult must understand the measure and be able to express their wishes. Toll-free 1 844 LECURATEUR. The Curateur public also runs free information sessions (some in French only).

entries.name: Adult Capacity and Decision-making Act (Nova Scotia Public Trustee)
entries.description: Nova Scotia's page on the law for adults who cannot make some or all decisions for themselves, for example because of a learning disability. It explains planning ahead with an Enduring Power of Attorney and a Personal Directive, and how a family member can apply to court to represent an adult only for the decisions they cannot make.
entries.cost_note: Capacity assessment costs apply; the government may pay up to $500 or $700 in cases of financial hardship.
entries.evidence: Recognize that adults may not be able to make some decisions because of a learning disability, mental health problems, brain injury, or for other reasons
entries.notes: Law in force since December 28, 2017; it replaced the Incompetent Persons Act, and old guardianship orders continue as representation orders. The email is the Public Trustee's general address.
